summary: OLSRv2 can assign metrics to links and use them to route by more than the fewest hops. This informational document provides a historic record of the rationale and design considerations behind how link metrics were included.

plainLanguage.summary: OLSRv2 lets a wireless network weigh its links, so a route can be chosen for quality rather than for hop count. This RFC explains why that was built into the protocol from the start, what properties the weights must have, and how they are carried in the messages.

questions: why does olsrv2 use link metrics
subtitle: Why OLSRv2 routes by a cost per link instead of by the fewest hops, and how that is measured.

tldr.problem: OLSRv1 finds routes with the fewest hops, which in practice is often a poor route. OLSRv2 was designed to let routers choose routes using a cost per link instead, and the design had to answer several non-obvious questions along the way.
tldr.mechanism: Link metrics in OLSRv2 are dimensionless and additive, one value per direction per pair of interfaces, with a separate neighbour metric for the best link between two routers. The metric values are carried in a compressed 12-bit exponent and mantissa form, and the receiving router is the one that decides the value.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that prescribes no behaviour. It is a record of why the choices were made, kept as a reference for when the same questions come up again. It also explains why link metrics had to be part of OLSRv2 itself rather than an extension.

today: RFC 7185 is an Informational RFC published in April 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the rationale record for the link metric design in OLSRv2 rather than a specification of behaviour.

sections.title: Why Metrics Are Part of the Protocol
sections.content:
OLSRv1 is a proactive routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks. It finds the shortest routes, defined as the minimum number of hops, from a router to every possible destination. Using only minimum hop routes may result in routes that are worse in practice, and one of the distinguishing features of OLSRv2 is the ability to select routes using link metrics other than the number of hops.

This document is a record of the considerations behind that decision. During the development of OLSRv2 the working group and the authors repeatedly discussed how and why particular choices were made, particularly at the metric integration level, and the document is offered as informational discussion of the motivation and the historic design choices, useful as a reference if the same questions arise again.

The decisive argument for putting metrics in the base protocol rather than in an extension is interoperability. OLSRv2 first determines local link metrics from one-hop neighbours, by a process outside OLSRv2, then distributes the metric values in HELLO and topology control messages, and finally forms routes with the minimum total link metric. If metric-based route selection had been an extension, routers that did not implement it would not recognise any link metric information and would go on using minimum hop-count routes. Routers that did implement it and routers that did not would then differ over their valuation of links and routes, which is the fundamental routing problem of looping. Link metrics were therefore included as standard in OLSRv2.
sections.plainLanguage: If metrics were optional, routers that used them and routers that did not would choose different routes and could loop. So the metrics had to be part of the protocol itself.

sections.title: When Fewer Hops Is Worse
sections.content:
The basic case for routes other than minimum hop ones is a small network with two paths from A to B. The minimum hop route goes through X, but if the links A to X and X to B are poor, for example low data rate or unreliable, while A to Y, Y to Z and Z to B are better, then the route through Y and Z may be preferred.

Other situations call for discouraging links even when avoiding them shows no obvious benefit to users. In a network with many short-range links and a few long-range ones, minimum hop routing sends heavy traffic over the long-range links, which is undesirable if those links achieve their range through reduced data rate or lower reliability. Even where the long-range links are no worse than the short ones, it may be better to reserve them for when their use is especially valuable, such as when one long-range link saves several short ones rather than the single link a minimum hop route needs.

A related case is the privileged relay, for example an aerial router in an otherwise ground-based network. The aerial router may have a link to many or all other routers, so all routers would try to send all their traffic through it. It may be important to keep that capacity for the cases where the aerial router is essential, such as when the ground-based part of the network is not connected. Link metrics offer a way to do this: give the aerial links maximum metric values, or give the ground links a value of 1 and make the sum of the aerial router's uplink and downlink metrics equal to N, so that using the aerial link only pays when it saves N ground links.

Other cases involve avoiding congested areas, routing around insecure routers, and discouraging routers that should not be used as relays because of limited battery power. OLSRv2 has a separate mechanism for the last of these, the willingness a router advertises, but there are cases where that cannot help and non-minimum hop routes could.

The RFC also separates link metrics from the optional link quality mechanism of the MANET neighbourhood discovery protocol. Link quality lets a router decline to use a link, on its own behalf and on behalf of all routers. It does not let the router use a link that is otherwise judged too low quality to be generally useful, as part of a route where no better links exist. The two mechanisms solve different problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Fewer hops is not always better. Metrics let a network prefer a longer path over bad links, or keep a costly long-range link in reserve for when it really helps, such as an aerial router that acts as a backup.

sections.title: The Properties of a Link Metric
sections.content:
Link metrics in OLSRv2 are dimensionless: they may correspond directly or indirectly to physical information such as delay, loss rate or data rate, but OLSRv2 does not use that knowledge, and producing the value is the job of a mechanism outside the protocol. They are additive, so the metric of a route is the sum of the metrics of its links, which means a low value must indicate a good link and a high value a bad one. They are directional, so the metric from A to B need not be the same as the metric from B to A, even over the same interfaces. And they are specific to a pair of OLSRv2 interfaces, so if there is more than one link from A to B each has its own metric in that direction.

On top of the link metrics there is an overall neighbor metric from A to B, which is the minimum of the link metrics between the two routers in the indicated direction, considering symmetric links only. It is undefined if there is no such symmetric link. HELLO messages may carry both link metrics and neighbor metrics, while topology control messages carry only neighbor metrics.

Several physical characteristics could define a metric, and each has its own quirks. Delay is straightforward, since it is naturally additive, though it does not by itself account for delays caused by routers rather than links, which can be divided among the incoming and outgoing links. Probability of loss is approximately additive when losses are small and independent, though it becomes pessimistic when they are not. Data rates are not additive at all, and they are backwards, being good when high, so a mapping that inverts the ordering has to be applied first, and that mapping can at best produce a metric that is merely acceptable to treat as additive. With three data rates of high, medium and low, metric values of 1, 10 and 100 achieve the wanted preference on the assumption that no route has more than 10 links; if routes can be longer, the range of values must grow, which is one reason the design preferred a wide dynamic range.

Within a single network all routers should use the same metric type, or the routes will be poor. How that is arranged is an administrative matter outside OLSRv2, and so is the physical meaning of the metrics, because new types may be added later, based on things like financial cost. Each type has a number, and the first one, type zero, is defined as a dimensionless metric with no predefined physical meaning. A router is configured with the single metric type it uses and recognises, without knowing what it represents.

OLSRv2 uses only symmetric, bidirectional links, and a key decision was whether each link should get one metric used in both directions or one per direction. Directional metrics were chosen, for two reasons. Links can genuinely differ in each direction, and in many cases the two ends of a link will naturally form different views of what the metric should be, so a single metric would need coordination between them that directional metrics avoid. With a single metric, the two ends would have to agree on its value, and if they did not, looping could occur.

Each router is therefore responsible for defining the metric in one direction only. The choice could have been either direction, as long as it is universal across the network. OLSRv2 uses the incoming direction, because a receiving router generally has more information to judge a link, for example received signal strength, interference levels and error-coding statistics. If A defines the metric of the link from B to A, then B must use A's definition of it in that direction.
sections.plainLanguage: A metric is a number with no units, and the numbers along a route add up. Each direction of a link has its own number, and the router that receives traffic on a link is the one that decides its value, because it can see the signal quality.

sections.title: The Link Metric Encoding
sections.content:
Link metric values are recorded in LINK_METRIC TLVs, using a compressed representation that occupies 12 bits. Using 12 bits is convenient because, with 4 flag bits of additional information, the result is a two-octet value field.

The 12 bits come from a modified exponent and mantissa form with two properties. The values represented are positive integers starting at 1. And the maximum value represented should be close to but less than 2^24, so that with a route limited to no more than 255 hops, the maximum route metric stays below 2^32 and can be stored in 32 bits, while the link metric itself fits in 24 bits.

In such a representation the values start at 1, are incremented by 1 up to 2^m, then take a further 2^m increments of 2, then a further 2^m increments of 4, and so on for 2^e sets of increments. The represented value is never in error by more than a half, if rounding, or one, if truncating, part in 2^m, and usually less. The position in the increment sequence is treated as a mantissa and denoted a, and the increment sequence number as an exponent and denoted b. The value represented by the pair (b,a) equals (2^m+a+1)2^b minus 2^m.

The maximum represented value has b at its largest and a at its largest, and is slightly less than 2^(2^e+m). The 24-bit limit is reached when 2^e+m is 24, and of the pairs that satisfy it, e = 4 and m = 8 was selected as most appropriate. That is the pair OLSRv2 uses, and it is where the 12 bits come from. Putting the flag bits first, the exponent bits go in the last four bits of the first octet and the mantissa bits in the second octet, so the 12 consecutive bits represent 256b+a in network byte order. Their ordering is the same as the ordering of the 24-bit values, which means two 12-bit metric fields can be compared for equality and ordering as if they were unsigned integers.

The four flag bits each represent one kind of metric, defined by its direction, incoming or outgoing, and whether it is a link metric or a neighbor metric, so a metric value may be of any combination of the four kinds.
sections.plainLanguage: The metric value is squeezed into 12 bits using a stepped exponent and mantissa, so that small values are exact and large ones are close enough. Four more bits say which direction and which kind of metric the number is.

sections.title: Flooding Relays and Routing Relays
sections.content:
OLSRv2 splits the two jobs that OLSRv1 gave to a single set of multipoint relays into two sets, flooding MPRs and routing MPRs. In both cases it is the MPR selectors that are actually used. Flooding MPRs decide which messages are forwarded, based on the MPR selector status of symmetric one-hop neighbours. Routing MPRs decide which links are advertised for routing, based on the topology information the router has collected.

Flooding MPR selection can ignore metrics and still meet the specification, which requires that a message transmitted by a router and retransmitted by all its flooding MPRs reaches all of the router's symmetric two-hop neighbours. But metrics can be usefully considered. In the RFC's example, if the metric represents probability of message loss, choosing the relay whose first hop has a higher metric but whose second hop has a much lower one maximises the chance that a message reaches the far node. But only looking at the second hop is also wrong, and the sum of the metrics is the appropriate measure to compare two candidate relays.

For routing, the specification requires that there is a two-hop route from each symmetric two-hop neighbour of the selecting router to the selecting router, with the intermediate router being a routing MPR. With an additive metric it is sufficient to require that these provide a minimum-distance two-hop route, not merely a two-hop one. The RFC's examples show the cost of this: link metrics may require a router to select more routing MPRs than without metrics, and even to select routing MPRs where it would otherwise need none, which means more and larger messages being generated and forwarded more often.

The two sets are often, but not always, different. They coincide when all metrics are equal. If the metrics are asymmetrically valued, because the two sets use opposite direction metrics, or if routers have several interfaces, since routing MPRs can ignore the interface while flooding MPRs cannot, the sets are particularly unlikely to match. Even with a symmetric metric and one interface per router, the ideal sets need not be equal, and neither is always a subset of the other: in one of the RFC's examples the set of routing MPRs serves as a set of flooding MPRs, but a non-minimal one, and in another the routing set must contain a router that the flooding set need not, while the flooding set must contain a router that the routing set need not.
sections.plainLanguage: OLSRv2 keeps two lists of helper routers. One decides which messages get forwarded, and one decides which links get advertised. Metrics affect the two differently, so the lists are usually not the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker can have an adverse impact on an OLSRv2 network by creating apparently valid messages that contain incorrect link metrics. This could influence the choice of routes or, in some cases, produce routing loops. The RFC calls this a more subtle and likely less effective attack than other forms of invalid message injection, which can add and remove more basic network information such as the existence of routers and links.

No significantly new security issues arose from including metrics in OLSRv2, and the defences against injecting invalid link metrics are the same as those against other forms of invalid message injection. The RFC also notes possible uses for link metrics in building security countermeasures that prefer links with better security properties, including better availability, but places that beyond the scope of both this document and the OLSRv2 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who can inject false metrics could steer traffic, so the defences are the ones already used against forged messages. Metrics could also be used to prefer safer links, but the RFC does not develop that idea.
